Rising AI adoption at ServiceNow (NYSE:NOW) hasn't kept the market from marking the shares down hard. ServiceNow stock trades at $97.93, down 5%. That leaves ServiceNow stock down 30% over the past month, with most of the damage arriving after the company's Q3 2026 report on October 28.

Sundry Photography / iStock Editorial via Getty Images

At its peak, ServiceNow stock reached a 52-week high of $175, a reminder of how much optimism it once carried. The debate over ServiceNow now centers on whether the slide is an overreaction to a noisy quarter or an early warning about growth.

How ServiceNow's October 28 Report Sparked the Selloff
NOW Earnings Explorer — 24/7 Wall St.

On October 28, ServiceNow reported Q3 revenue of $4.11 billion, up 20.5% year over year (YoY) and ahead of the $4.09 billion consensus estimate. ServiceNow's adjusted earnings per share (EPS) of $1 missed expectations of $1.02, ending a six-quarter run of beats.

Moreover, acquisition costs pressured the company's GAAP operating margin to 9.5% from 17% a year earlier. Sellers moved quickly, taking ServiceNow stock from $154.60 when the results came out to $105.12 a day later.

This leaves a straightforward question for you as an investor: Is the current US$214.94 price tag adequately supported by the earnings power of the underlying business?

Over the past 5 years the stock has fallen 28.3%, which puts the spotlight firmly on whether the earnings profile now lines up with that weaker share performance.

The planned acquisition of voice AI company Cresta and a debt funded US$25b buyback program can reshape how investors think about Salesforce's future profit mix and financing costs, and therefore what multiple of earnings they are willing to pay.

Is Salesforce a Bargain on Earnings?

The P/E ratio fits Salesforce because investors often anchor software valuations on earnings power rather than assets. At roughly 18.3x earnings, the stock trades well below the broader Software industry average of about 30.3x and also under the peer group near 45.6x, which points to a marked discount on this headline metric.

title: Salesforce Sinks as S&P Cuts Its Rating to A on Deals and a $25 Billion Buyback
detail:
Salesforce Sinks as S&P Cuts Its Rating to A on Deals and a $25 Billion Buyback
Rexielyn Diaz
Tue, November 10, 2026 at 6:49 AM MST 5 min read
CRM
NOW
BRZE
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Salesforce Sinks as S&P Cuts Its Rating to A on Deals and a $25 Billion Buyback ©@Blue Planet Studio from Getty Images via Canva, @AndreyPopov from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

S&P cut Salesforce's credit rating to A from A+ last week, citing rising acquisition activity and shareholder returns, while keeping a stable outlook.

Salesforce agreed to buy Braze for about $5.66 billion in October and Cresta in November, after a $3.6 billion deal for Fin earlier this year.

Informatica supplies slightly more than 4 points of Salesforce's guided growth, while ServiceNow grew revenue 20.5% last quarter.

The third-quarter report, expected in early December, has to show the organic revenue reacceleration management keeps promising.

Salesforce (CRM:NYSE) took a credit downgrade last week, and you can see the reason in its deal log.

S&P Global Ratings cut the company to A from A+ on November 4. The agency pointed to rising acquisition activity and shareholder returns. It kept a stable outlook, though, and still expects subscription revenue and earnings to grow.

The downgrade came two days after Salesforce agreed to buy Cresta, a private voice AI company. Two weeks before that, it struck a deal for Braze (BRZE:NASDAQ), the customer engagement platform, at about $5.66 billion in cash. Braze shares jumped more than 50% that day.

Salesforce stock slid through most of last week. Meanwhile, ServiceNow (NOW:NYSE) just grew revenue 20.5% in its third quarter, nearly double Salesforce's pace.

Three deals and a downgrade

The leverage built up in stages this year:

In March, Salesforce sold $25 billion of senior notes to fund a $25 billion accelerated share repurchase.

In June, it agreed to buy Fin for about $3.6 billion, alongside a separate deal for Contentful.

Braze and Cresta followed in October and November. Salesforce didn't disclose Cresta's price, and The Information reported it at $2.7 billion.

Moody's had already trimmed Salesforce to A2 in March over the debt-funded buyback. So S&P is mostly catching up to a balance sheet that changed months ago.

Salesforce (CRM): total debt and net debt, quarterly, $ billions, Q2 FY2025–Q2 FY2026 (TIKR)

Both agencies still rate the company solidly investment grade. Yet the bill isn't finished, because Braze and Cresta are both expected to close in fiscal 2028, which starts in February.

Buying growth while waiting for it

On paper, each deal fills a gap. Braze brings real-time messaging for about 2,770 customers to Marketing Cloud, and Cresta adds voice agents used by Marriott and Comcast to Service Cloud.

Shay Boloor of Futurum Equities told Reuters that Braze gives Salesforce "a real-time engagement layer that its marketing business has historically lacked."

Organic growth is the harder question. Second-quarter revenue rose 11% to $11.3 billion, but Informatica contributed $456 million. Third-quarter guidance calls for 11% to 12% growth, and slightly more than 4 points of that also comes from Informatica.
